idiom_name: const member functions + free functions returning values
implementation_notes: The classic C++ realization: a query is a const member function or a free function that takes const references and returns a new value, while a command is a non-const member function that returns void. The compiler checks the object part - a const member function cannot modify *this - so the query/command split is visible in the declaration. The guarantee stops at this object: mutable members, data reached through pointers and globals can still change, so keep it when the model is built around encapsulated objects and reach for the compile-time variant when the computation must also be usable in constant expressions.
pitfalls: const on a member function protects this only: mutable members, pointed-to data, caches and globals can still change, so a const query may remain observably impure.
const_cast and accessors returning references to internals (const T& get() const) hand mutation back to the caller and void the guarantee.
const says nothing about thread safety: a const function that reads a member another thread writes is a data race, not a pure query.

variants.name: constexpr pure functions evaluated at compile time (C++11 and later)
variants.implementation_notes: A constexpr function can be evaluated at compile time whenever its arguments are constant expressions, and the language forbids side effects and calls to non-constexpr code on that path - so purity is actually checked there. C++14 relaxed the single-return-statement body restriction and C++20 added consteval for immediately-evaluated functions. Use it for invariants, unit conversions and lookup-table generation and verify results with static_assert; the function remains dual-use, so calls with runtime arguments are ordinary unchecked calls. Prefer this variant over plain const-correctness when the toolchain is at least C++11 and the results feed other compile-time decisions.
pitfalls: A constexpr function is dual-use: called with runtime arguments it is an ordinary function, and nothing then checks that it stayed free of hidden reads.
Undefined behaviour on the constant-evaluated path (division by zero, out-of-bounds indexing, uninitialised reads) is a compile error, so compile-time helpers must handle every input.
